title: The month of numbers you do not have
hook: Installs a memory-reporting agent in all three clouds and opens a thirty-day sampling window, because none of them reports guest working set without one.
scope: None of the three clouds reports guest memory from the hypervisor, so the working-set figures a purchase order needs do not exist until an agent is running: the CloudWatch agent on AWS, the Azure Monitor agent behind a data collection rule, and the Ops Agent on Google Cloud, which is the only one of the three that ships memory in its default configuration. Adds per-container working set and IOPS from the managed Kubernetes metrics you already collect, and records what cannot be measured at all — burstable credit balances, page cache against anonymous memory, and the CI minutes that never appeared as instances. About four days of work spread across a thirty-day window, and the window is why this is the first Move in the book.
corrections_applied: Old Move 01 conflated measurement, sizing and the purchase order into one Move; the measurement half is separated here and the purchase order becomes Move 20.
Old Move 01 was AWS-only ('ninety days of CloudWatch percentiles'); the agent that must be installed is now named on each of the three clouds, with the one default-on case stated.
The collection window is stated as thirty days and made the gating item, rather than an unexplained ninety.
Hook converted to third-person indicative, per the critic's systematic voice-drift finding.

title: What a vCPU is actually worth
leaving: The vCPU as a unit of purchase
hook: Converts a month of samples into a derated core requirement, and corrects the derate on the families where a vCPU is a whole core rather than a thread.
scope: Converts a month of samples into a derated requirement using p95 and p99 per workload rather than the fleet peak, then corrects the vCPU count for what a vCPU actually was on the family you ran. It is one SMT thread on most x86 families, and one whole physical core on Graviton, on Google's C4A, T2D, T2A, N4A and H3, and on Azure's Cobalt 100 Dpsv6 and Epsv6 series; applying the halving derate to those over-buys by a factor of two, which is the most expensive single error available in this Part. Burstable families — the t-series, Azure B-series, and e2-medium and below — report utilisation against a credit budget rather than against a core, so their samples are discarded and those workloads re-measured on a non-burstable shape. About five days.
corrections_applied: Critic's 'wrong' item on old Move 01: 'an EC2 vCPU is one hyperthread' is false for Graviton and for the SMT-disabled families. The exceptions are now enumerated on all three clouds and the over-buy is quantified as a factor of two.
Adds the burstable-family correction the old Move gestured at ('a t-family instance was borrowing credits') but never resolved: those samples are discarded, not derated.
The derate is settled in its own Move before any component is chosen, so no later Iron Move inherits an uncorrected core count.

title: The estate nobody sizes
leaving: Non-production capacity that costs nothing when it is switched off, and hosted CI runners
hook: Sizes dev, staging and CI from the same month of samples, because on hardware you own idle non-production costs exactly what busy non-production costs.
scope: Dev, staging, the non-production cluster and CI together run between a third and the whole of production again, and cost models omit them because non-production scaled to zero overnight and hosted runners — CodeBuild, Cloud Build, Microsoft-hosted Azure Pipelines agents — never appeared as instances at all. Sizes them from the same month of data plus billed build minutes, cache and artefact storage, and states plainly that on your own hardware idle non-production costs the same as busy non-production. Decides here whether the non-production cluster shares production machines or gets its own smaller ones, because that answer changes the machine count in Move 11; the cluster itself is stood up in Part III. About four days.
corrections_applied: Critic's 'missing' item that no Move builds the second cluster while three Moves assume it: the hardware for it is sized here and the build is handed explicitly to Part III rather than being left implicit.

Hosted CI runners are named on all three clouds; the old manifest sized 'dev, staging and CI' on the same page as everything else and never said that hosted runners appear as build minutes rather than as instances.

title: Cores against clock, and the licence that decides it
hook: Picks socket count, generation and vendor against the derated requirement, then re-checks the answer against per-core licensing, which frequently inverts it.
scope: Picks socket count, generation and vendor against the derated requirement, then checks the answer against per-core licensing. Oracle counts every physical core in the host at the 0.5 x86 core factor unless the partitioning is one Oracle has approved as hard, SQL Server per-core licenses every core on the server with a four-core minimum per processor, and Windows Server carries an eight-core minimum per processor and sixteen per server — so a dense dual-socket part can cost more in licences than in silicon, and a licensed workload wants few fast cores on a machine of its own. One socket is usually right for a Kubernetes node and two only for memory capacity or PCIe lanes; the generation behind is worth buying when the discount exceeds the performance-per-watt gap over three years of power you now pay for directly. About five days, most of it spent getting the licensing position in writing rather than benchmarking.
corrections_applied: Critic's 'missing' item that licensing can veto a migration: the core-factor and per-core minimums are settled in Part I where they change the purchase order, and the database and Windows estates that depend on them are Move 78.
Replaces the old manifest's implicit assumption that a node is chosen on price and core count alone.

title: SMT, NUMA, and the workload that notices
hook: Settles SMT and the NUMA layout before latency-sensitive work arrives, and sets the kubelet policies without which two containers can share one physical core.
scope: Decides SMT on or off and fixes the NUMA layout before any latency-sensitive workload arrives, because the instance shapes you were buying hid both. On a chiplet EPYC the NUMA-per-socket setting and the last-level-cache boundary matter more than the socket count, and Kubernetes honours none of it unless the kubelet runs the CPU manager static policy with the full-pcpus-only option and the topology manager set to single-numa-node — without which two containers can be pinned to the two halves of one physical core and contend for its L1 and L2. Records the symptom of each wrong setting, since these faults appear only above a load threshold and present as an application regression. About three days; the settings survive a reboot, but the core count they imply does not survive the purchase order.
corrections_applied: Reversibility is stated honestly in two halves: the BIOS and kubelet settings revert on a reboot, the core count they imply is baked into Move 11's machine count.
Adds the kubelet-side requirement the old manifest never named, so the hardware decision and the Kubernetes configuration that makes it real are settled together.

title: Memory is what runs out first
hook: Sizes memory from measured working set plus reserves, rounds up to a population that fills every channel, and orders it first because it is the longest lead.
scope: Sizes memory from the measured working set plus page cache, kubelet and system reserved, and the eviction threshold, then rounds up to a DIMM population that fills every channel — twelve per socket on current EPYC and on the twelve-channel Xeon 6 parts, eight on the rest — because a half-populated channel map costs bandwidth out of proportion to the capacity saved. Two DIMMs per channel buys capacity at a documented speed drop, and the twelve-channel parts are one DIMM per channel only, so 'add memory later' is a decision made at purchase rather than deferred by it. Memory is also the long-lead, price-volatile line: HBM allocation has pushed server RDIMM lead times and contract prices well outside their historical range, which makes it the item to order first and the one whose quote expires soonest, so the figure is re-checked against a live quote rather than taken from this page. About three days.
corrections_applied: The 1DPC constraint on twelve-channel parts is stated, so the reader does not plan a memory upgrade into slots that do not exist.
The DRAM market claim is written as a direction with a re-check instruction rather than as a price or a lead time that will be stale before the book is read.

title: One rack unit or two, and the watts it draws
hook: Chooses chassis and supplies from the CPU and DIMM population, and produces the per-node and per-rack draw the facility contract in Part II is written against.
scope: Chooses the chassis and the supplies in it: 1U against 2U for drive bays, PCIe slots, fan power and cooling headroom; rack depth and rail kit against a cabinet not yet signed for in Part II; front against rear I/O so that cabling and airflow agree rather than fight. Titanium-rated supplies are generally 200 to 240 V input only and peak in efficiency near half load, so the supply is sized against measured draw rather than badge rating, and two supplies fed from one busbar is not redundancy — it is one feed and two failure points. Multi-node and blade chassis are refused, because a shared midplane, shared supplies and vendor-locked spares move the failure domain from the node to the enclosure. About three days, and the output is the per-node and per-rack draw Part II contracts against.
corrections_applied: The power figure the facility contract is written against is produced in Part I, correcting the old order in which old Move 04 signed for cabinet power alongside the bill of materials rather than after it.

title: The way in when the machine will not boot
leaving: The provider's serial console and boot diagnostics
hook: Treats the management controller as a purchase-order line, tests Redfish on a loan unit, and finds which console features sit behind a licence before delivery.
scope: Treats the baseboard management controller as a line on the purchase order rather than something the chassis happens to include, because it is the replacement for EC2 Serial Console and Instance Connect, for the Azure serial console and boot diagnostics, and for the Compute Engine interactive serial console. Tests Redfish conformance against a loan unit rather than a datasheet, and establishes whether remote console and virtual media sit behind a licence — they do on Dell iDRAC Enterprise, on HPE iLO Advanced, and behind Supermicro's DCMS key — since discovering that after delivery means paying per machine under time pressure. Records the firmware support horizon and how updates are delivered, which is the number that actually dates the platform. About two days.
corrections_applied: Old Move 05 bundled the BMC purchase decision with the management VLAN and the break-glass drill; the purchase-order half is settled here in Part I and the VLAN, credential rotation and drill are Move 40.
The provider console being left is named on all three clouds rather than AWS only.

title: The drive you are allowed to put etcd on
reversible: Per drive, at the cost of a Ceph rebuild
hook: Fixes interface, form factor and endurance, and makes power-loss protection a hard requirement, because a drive without it is a quorum defect you have bought.
scope: Fixes interface and device: NVMe for anything that matters, SATA only for cold bulk, SAS only where an existing enclosure forces it. Power-loss protection is a hard requirement rather than a preference — a drive without it must genuinely flush on every fsync, which turns etcd's write path from microseconds into milliseconds and makes a consumer SSD a quorum outage waiting for load. Form factor is chosen with care because compatibility runs one way: a U.3 drive falls back into a U.2 bay and a U.2 drive does not work in a U.3 bay, so a mixed order can arrive unusable. Sets the endurance class in drive-writes-per-day against the measured write rate, noting that DWPD is quoted over the warranty term and drives with different warranties are not comparable on that number alone, and names the wear metrics to alarm on: percentage used, available spare against its own threshold, media and data integrity errors, and unsafe shutdowns. About four days.
corrections_applied: Reversibility is stated per drive and priced as a Ceph rebuild rather than left as an unqualified 'Immediately'.
The U.2 and U.3 compatibility direction is stated explicitly and verified, since getting it backwards produces an order that cannot be racked.

title: How much flash, and where it sits
leaving: Block volumes that grow with an API call
hook: Turns the measured capacity requirement into drives against Ceph's replication and its nearfull thresholds, and separates the etcd, local-NVMe and OSD tiers.
scope: Turns the measured capacity requirement into drives, counting what Ceph actually takes: three-way replication triples raw consumption, erasure coding does not but costs recovery, and both need free space held back, since Ceph's defaults warn at eighty-five per cent, stop backfill at ninety and stop accepting writes at ninety-five — a cluster planned to sit at nearfull passes a healthy-day check and fails during the recovery it was bought for. Separates the tiers, because they have different endurance and different sizes: a mirrored pair of small high-endurance drives for etcd, local NVMe for the single-writer databases that will not sit on Ceph, and the OSD drives themselves. Buys chassis with bays deliberately left empty, because capacity that grew with an API call now grows only when somebody walks to the rack. About three days.
corrections_applied: The storage tiering is written against the book's committed stack — Ceph under Rook with local NVMe underneath it — rather than surveying arrays or alternative CSI drivers, and a SAN is refused outright.
Reversibility is bounded honestly: adding drives is cheap until the bays are full, after which it is a chassis purchase.

title: Headroom, and the number of machines you order
leaving: Elastic node capacity: cluster autoscaling and node auto-provisioning
hook: Multiplies the node shape by the derated requirement, adds the losses per-hour pricing hid, and produces the machine count, rack-unit budget and total draw.
scope: Multiplies the node shape by the derated requirement and adds the losses that per-hour pricing hid: kubelet and system reserved, the Ceph and CNI daemonsets, bin-packing waste measured against the largest single pod you run, and enough spare capacity to lose a whole node — or a whole rack — without evicting production. Fixes the control-plane count at three or five and states which failure domain each one sits in. Produces the machine count, the rack-unit budget and the total power draw the Part II facility contract is written against, and is where the reader confronts the honest cost of the exercise: capacity is now bought in whole servers with a lead time rather than requested from an API. About four days.
corrections_applied: Depends on Move 03, so the non-production and CI estate is inside the machine count rather than discovered after the order is placed.
The refusal to size from the instance types you were renting is stated here, where the count is actually produced.

title: Two switches, and the spine you do not need yet
reversible: Until the second rack is cabled
hook: Chooses the fabric topology from measured east-west traffic, refuses a spine below four racks, and records whether the fabric runs MLAG or BGP to the host.
scope: Chooses the fabric topology from measured east-west traffic rather than from a reference diagram. One to three racks is a pair of top-of-rack switches with a peer link and no spine at all; leaf-spine earns its place when rack count or cabling makes the direct mesh unmanageable, and buying it early costs ports, optics, power and rack units for years before anything uses them. Computes the oversubscription ratio from real numbers and sets uplink count from it, then records whether the fabric will run MLAG or BGP to the host, because Cilium's design in Move 45 and the service-address advertisement in Move 96 both depend on that answer. About four days.
corrections_applied: The MLAG-or-BGP answer is named as a prerequisite of two specific later Moves, closing a dependency the old manifest left implicit between the fabric and the CNI.

title: The switch, and the software running on it
hook: Buys tier-one merchant-silicon leaves running a supported network operating system, and checks the quoted licence tier for the routing features assumed.
scope: The book buys tier-one merchant-silicon switches running a vendor network operating system, and the recommendation is Arista EOS on Trident-class leaf hardware, because its BGP and EVPN behaviour is documented, supported and dull, and a six-person team should not be debugging a forwarding plane at 03:00. A commercially supported Enterprise SONiC distribution is the alternative where procurement requires an open NOS; community SONiC and Cumulus Linux are named and set aside, the latter because Cumulus 5 dropped Broadcom silicon and runs on Spectrum only. Checks port count and speed against three years of growth, buffer depth against the microbursts you measured rather than a rule of thumb, and — the detail that catches people — whether the base licence tier on the exact SKU being quoted includes the routing features you are assuming. About two weeks, including loan units, quotes and a licensing answer in writing.
corrections_applied: One NOS is recommended and the alternatives are named in a line, rather than surveyed, per the book's commitment to an opinionated stack.

Applies the book's licence test to the network estate: the feature tier on the quoted SKU is checked in writing before the order, the same discipline the critic asked for on Terraform and Vault elsewhere.
The Cumulus silicon-support position is verified and stated rather than left as a name on a list.

title: The card, the driver, and the kernel you will run
leaving: The provider's paravirtual network interface and its single driver
reversible: Per node, at the cost of a card swap and a reboot
hook: Chooses the network card against the Talos kernel rather than a datasheet, because there is no DKMS and no third place a driver can come from.
scope: Chooses the network card against the Talos kernel rather than against a datasheet. Talos enforces kernel module signatures and has no DKMS, so a driver is either in the base kernel or in an official system extension and there is no third option — verify the exact card and its firmware requirement, not the family, before the order goes out, because there is no recovery path on the far side. Two ports on one card is one PCIe device and one failure domain, so genuine redundancy is two cards where the workload justifies the slot; 25G to the host with 100G uplinks is the sensible floor today. Refuses SR-IOV and RDMA for a general Kubernetes estate, because they bypass the eBPF datapath that Move 60's east-west policy is enforced in and buy nothing measurable outside HPC and dedicated storage fabrics. About three days.
corrections_applied: The host OS is Talos and the driver constraint is stated as a hard purchasing constraint, rather than the old manifest's open choice of host operating system.
The SR-IOV refusal is tied to the specific later Move whose policy enforcement it would break.

title: Copper inside the rack, glass between them
reversible: Immediately, at the cost of re-coding or re-ordering
hook: Orders cabling and optics once both ends exist, settles connector polish and vendor coding at order time, and buys one spare of every type in the same order.
scope: Passive direct-attach copper inside a rack out to about three metres, active optical or discrete transceivers beyond it, and OS2 single-mode between racks rather than multimode, because the incremental cost is small and it does not need replacing at the next speed step. Records connector and polish per link — duplex LC for FR and LR, MPO-12 with APC for parallel single-mode — since a UPC patch lead in an APC channel presents as a marginal optic and is diagnosed last. Optics carry vendor identity in EEPROM and switch vendors may warn, block or decline support on third-party modules, so the coding is chosen at order time and confirmed against the support contract, and breakout cables need the port mode configured before they will link at all. Buys one spare of every optic and cable type in the same order. About two days.
corrections_applied: Ordered only after both ends of every link exist, which the old manifest's single hardware Move could not express.

title: The network that works when the network is down
hook: Buys the out-of-band estate as hardware in its own right, on its own uplink and power, because the management controller rides the network you are fixing.
scope: Buys the out-of-band estate as hardware in its own right: a small management switch, a serial console server with ports for every switch and enough servers to matter, and their own uplink and power that do not traverse the production fabric, the cluster or the same supply. This is what remains when the production switch pair is itself the fault, and it is both the cheapest line on the bill of materials and the one most often cut on the grounds that the management controller is enough — which it is not, because that controller is reached over the network you are trying to fix. The management VLAN, the credential rotation and the break-glass drill are Move 40; this Move only ensures the hardware exists to build them on. About two days.
corrections_applied: Separated cleanly from Move 40 so that the hardware is on the purchase order in Part I and the operational path is built in Part III, which old Move 05 ran together.

title: Who you buy from, and what is safe to buy used
leaving: The hardware refresh someone else did for you
reversible: 14 to 30 days, per the vendor's return window
hook: Prices the specification three ways, reads the warranty for response against restore, and treats lead time rather than unit price as the schedule risk.
scope: Prices the same specification three ways — tier one with next-business-day on-site parts, a whitebox ODM at a lower price with return-to-base, and refurbished — and reads the warranty for response against restore, parts-only against labour, and what happens in year four when the platform reaches end of service life and spares stop being made. Refurbished is legitimate for chassis, CPUs, switches and optics, and is where a memory price spike will push you, but never for flash, batteries or supercapacitors; a used purchase needs a written inspection list covering SMART percentage used and power-on hours, the BMC event log, the firmware level and whether it can still be updated, and whether the serial number is still entitled to vendor support. Lead time is the schedule risk rather than price: memory is the long pole, quoted build times move by months, and a quote is not a delivery date. About three weeks, including quotes, reference calls and a support-entitlement check per serial.
corrections_applied: This Move buys hardware warranty only; commercial support contracts for the open-source stack are Move 112, which is the critic's 'missing' item and a different question with a different vendor.
Reversibility is stated as the actual return window rather than as an unqualified 'Immediately'.

title: Nothing carries production until it has been made to fail
reversible: Immediately; this is the last cheap moment
hook: Writes the acceptance suite before the order is placed and makes passing it a term of the purchase order, so a failed machine is a return rather than an argument.
scope: Writes the acceptance suite before the order is placed and makes passing it a term of the purchase order, so a machine that fails is a return rather than an argument. Every node runs a multi-pass memory test, fio at the workload's own profile plus a full-surface pass per drive, a sustained CPU and thermal soak with inlet and exhaust temperature logged, and both network ports at line rate on the cable that will actually be used. Failure is defined in advance and in writing: any machine check, any correctable ECC trend rather than a single event, any PCIe correctable-error storm, any thermal throttle at rated inlet temperature. This is also where the front-matter homelab stops being representative — three refurbished desktops under a desk proved the software estate and proved nothing about ECC behaviour, dual-feed supplies, bonded links across two switches, BMC recovery or drive endurance under Ceph. About one week to write the suite, and about one week of elapsed time per batch to run it.
corrections_applied: Names the point at which the front-matter homelab on-ramp stops being representative, which the brief requires Part I to state and the old manifest never did.

title: The shelf, and the failure rates you stock against
hook: Sets on-site spares from population and published failure rates, stocks a whole cold spare node, and counts the consumables nobody budgets for.
scope: Sets on-site spares from population and published failure rates rather than instinct: the largest public fleet dataset has reported annualised drive failure in the region of one to one and a half per cent for several years, and it is a disk fleet rather than a flash one, which is stated so the reader discounts it accordingly. Fans and power supplies are the commodity failures and DIMMs are the one that hides for weeks as a correctable-error trend. Stocks a whole cold spare node, which beats any RMA on time to service and is the only spare that covers a fault you cannot yet diagnose, and counts the consumables nobody budgets — rails, cage nuts, patch leads, optics, labels and a labelled bay map — while recording the RMA turnaround the contract promises against the one the vendor achieves, because those are different numbers and only one of them belongs in the runbook. About two days, and the output is a line on the bill of materials rather than an afterthought.
corrections_applied: Critic's ordering finding on old Moves 62 and 63: the pair is split, and spares stocking becomes a bill-of-materials line here while the inventory, RMA loop and the 03:00 disk stay in Part VII as Moves 110 and 111, in that order.
The failure-rate figure is attributed to published fleet data and its limitation — disk rather than flash — is stated, rather than being printed as a bare statistic.

title: The bill of materials
leaving: Committed-spend discounts on rented compute
hook: Assembles every Iron decision into a document a supplier can quote against, and sets the three-year cost frame the rest of the book is judged against.
scope: Assembles every preceding decision into a document a supplier can quote against: SKUs, quantities, unit prices, lead times, firmware baselines, per-rack power draw, the rack-unit budget, spares, the acceptance terms, and an explicit exclusion list for the cabinet, the PDUs and the cross-connects, which are Part II. States the order sequence rather than a single date, because memory and optics have the longest lead times and a switch without transceivers is a paperweight. Sets the three-year cost frame the rest of the book is judged against, and names the renewal date of the committed-spend discount you are choosing not to renew — a Savings Plan or Reserved Instance on AWS, a Committed Use Discount on Google Cloud, a Reservation or savings plan on Azure — which is the real deadline. About one week.
corrections_applied: Old Move 01 opened the book with the bill of materials and derived it from ninety days of AWS percentiles in a single Move; it becomes the destination of Part I instead, assembled from nineteen decisions that each had to be settled first.
The committed-spend discount being left is named on all three clouds rather than as EC2 Savings Plans and Reserved Instances alone.
Reversibility is 'No' honestly: this is the document that becomes a purchase order, and every earlier Iron Move is reversible until it is signed.

title: What the three machines under the desk cannot tell you
hook: Writes down on one page what a three-machine desk cluster proved and what it did not, and attaches each remaining gap by name to the Move that closes it.
scope: The front-matter on-ramp proved the software estate on three refurbished machines for about $1,840, and readers arrive from it believing the migration is de-risked. This Move writes down, on one page, what it did not prove: sustained thermals at real duty rather than a ten-minute benchmark, a switch fabric wider than one box, drive endurance measured in drive-writes-per-day against a year of writes, dual power supplies, out-of-band access from another city, and the four-week wait for a replacement part. Each gap is named against the Move in this Part or the next that closes it, so the list is a map rather than a warning. About three days, most of it spent reading numbers off a desk cluster that has been left at full load for a week.
corrections_applied: Opens Part II with the on-ramp's limits, which the previous manifest never stated anywhere: old Move 02 went straight from the purchase order to a landing decision.
Keeps the homelab boundary out of Part I's acceptance Move (Move 18) and restates it here in facility terms, so neither Move carries the whole argument alone.

title: The four places the machines could live
leaving: The region-and-zone abstraction
hook: Prices retail colocation, wholesale space, rented dedicated servers and a room you already occupy against the committed power figure, with staff time counted.
scope: Prices the four landing options on one page: retail colocation, wholesale space, rented dedicated servers, and a room in a building you occupy. Each gets capital cost, monthly cost at the committed power figure from Move 20, the staff time it consumes, the lead time before the first machine boots, and the cost of getting out again. The staffing arithmetic is carried here from Part VII rather than left until Move 113, because a rota that covers nights and weekends without attrition needs a headcount that changes which of the four options is affordable, and this is the last point at which the reader can act on that answer. A mixed landing is treated as a real answer rather than indecision, because rented metal in another city is usually the cheapest disaster-recovery target you will ever price. About two weeks, most of it waiting on quotations from four suppliers.
corrections_applied: Absorbs the landing-model half of old Move 02 and drops its cluster-count content, which now belongs to Move 03 (sizing) and Move 51 (building the second cluster).

Applies the critic's finding that old Move 66's staffing viability arithmetic sits 64 Moves after the purchase order: it is pulled forward to here, against each landing option, and Move 113 keeps only the rota's construction.

Resolves the critic's objection that old Move 02's reversible 'Immediately' was false. The decision Move is now genuinely reversible because nothing is signed in it; the irreversible commitments are separated into Move 28 (power schedule), Move 30 (term and notice) and Move 34 (import).
leaving generalised from a named provider's regions and availability zones to the abstraction itself.

title: The room in your own building
hook: Sets out the narrow case for a room in a building you occupy, then prices the suppression, detection, consent and insurance most estimates leave out.
scope: Sets out the narrow case in which an on-premises room is defensible: you own or hold a long lease on the building, there is a second supply from a different substation, the plant room has the structural capacity for the cooling, and somebody's job title contains the word facilities. It then prices what most estimates omit — clean-agent or water-mist suppression and its annual test, detection designed to BS 6266 or NFPA 75, planning consent and fuel-storage approval for a generator, an insurance schedule an underwriter has actually seen, and a maintenance contract behind each of those. The arithmetic, not the tone, is what concludes that most companies should not. About one week, worth spending even when the answer is no.
corrections_applied: New Move: the previous manifest offered only colocation against rented metal and never examined the on-premises room, which is the option readers most often propose and the one that fails on costs nobody quotes.
Placed immediately after the four options so the reader who wants it is talked out of it by arithmetic rather than by tone.

title: The second site you are not building this year
hook: Refuses a second site in year one, names the three conditions that change the answer, and buys a costed restore into rented metal in another city instead.
scope: A second site doubles the facility bill, the cabling, the spares pool and the change surface, in exchange for protection against a failure that a well-chosen facility already makes rare. This Move names the three conditions under which you build it anyway — a regulator that requires it, a signed customer commitment that names it, or revenue per hour above the annual cost of the second site — and otherwise buys a costed, rehearsed restore into rented metal in another city. It also disposes of the two false second sites: a second cabinet in the same building, and a second building on the same substation and the same fibre route. About three days, ending in a written decision and a budget line for the year in which it changes.
corrections_applied: Absorbs the second-site half of old Move 02 and states it as a refusal with named conditions rather than a deferral, so the reader has something to test rather than a promise to revisit.

Answers the critic's complaint that old Move 65 reached the object store only transitively: the refusal here is settled again in Move 115 against a measured rebuild time, and Move 115 now names the store directly.
Placed beside the landing decision it constrains rather than 63 Moves later.

title: The flood plain, the fault line and the grid
hook: Checks the address rather than the brochure: flood history, seismic category, the substation behind each feed, and the fibre routes drawn on a map.
scope: Checks the address rather than the brochure: the national flood map and the building's own flood history, the seismic design category and whether the cabinets need bracing that has to be ordered with them, the substation feeding the site and whether the second feed genuinely comes from a different one, and the fibre entries drawn on a map rather than described as diverse. It adds the distances that matter — road time for a person carrying a part, and fibre distance to your users and to the cloud region you are leaving, at roughly one millisecond of round trip per hundred kilometres of glass, measured along the real path rather than the great circle. A site that fails this cannot be repaired by better contract terms, which is why it runs before the contract is read. About four days, including one site visit and one request for as-built utility drawings the facility would rather not send.
corrections_applied: New Move: the previous manifest signed a facility in old Move 04 without ever checking the address, the grid behind it or the diversity of its fibre entries.
States the latency figure as propagation along the real path, avoiding the common error of quoting great-circle distance.

title: Carrier neutrality and the cross-connect price list
hook: Counts the carriers that will sell at your volume and prices every cross-connect you will need across three years against the facility's own list.
scope: Asks for the list of carriers with live fibre in the meet-me room, then asks which of them will actually sell at your volume, which is a much shorter list. Prices every cross-connect you will need across three years — two transit providers, a peering fabric port, the private interconnect back to the cloud you are leaving, one per additional cabinet — against the facility's own price list, commonly $50 to $350 a month each plus installation, recurring forever and usually outside the cabinet price. Notes that the authorisation for a cloud on-ramp has a shelf life: an AWS letter of authorisation and connecting facility assignment expires ninety days after issue if the cross-connect is not completed, so it is ordered when the cabinet is ready and not before. About one week.
corrections_applied: New Move: cross-connects appeared in old Move 04 as a line item with no price list, no carrier count and no bearing on site selection, which left Part VI's transit negotiation (Move 93) resting on a building that might hold one seller.
Adds the ninety-day expiry on the cloud on-ramp authorisation, which the previous manifest did not carry anywhere and which sequences the order against cabinet readiness.

title: What a tier rating promises, and what it does not
hook: Separates tier topology from tier certification and from the similarly numbered parallel schemes, and retires the availability percentages quoted beside them.
scope: Separates three things a sales deck runs together. Uptime Institute tier topology describes redundancy and concurrent maintainability and nothing else; tier certification comes in three distinct forms covering the design documents, the constructed facility and operational sustainability, of which only the second says the building was built the way it was drawn; and the parallel schemes with confusingly similar numbering, ANSI/TIA-942 Rated 1 to 4 and EN 50600 availability classes 1 to 4, are different standards with different scopes. It also retires the availability percentages still quoted against each tier, which Uptime Institute removed from the standard in 2009 and which never constituted a guarantee. The output is a question list for the tour and a note of which certificate, if any, the facility actually holds. About two days.
corrections_applied: New Move: old Move 04 bought cabinet space without ever telling the reader which facility claims to discount, and the tier percentages are the most repeated false number in this field.
Verified that Uptime Institute removed the expected-downtime figures from the tier standard in 2009; the claim is stated as a removal rather than as a guarantee that was broken.
Placed before the power schedule so the reader knows which claims to discount when the numbers arrive.

title: Committed kilowatts, metered kilowatts and the derate
hook: Reads the power schedule rather than the price, and fixes the billing model, the committed figure and the continuous-load derate in writing.
scope: Reads the power schedule rather than the price. Establishes which of three billing models is in front of you — a flat charge against a committed figure, metered consumption with a committed floor, or a hybrid with an overage rate — and what the facility does when you exceed the commitment: alarm, invoice, or trip the breaker. Fixes the derate in writing, because the eighty per cent continuous-load convention is an artefact of US wiring code with no direct equivalent in BS 7671 or IEC 60364, so a European facility may sell against the full breaker rating where a US one will not, and the only number that matters is the one the contract says you may draw continuously. Ends with the committed figure for the first cabinet and a written right to increase it mid-term. About one week, half of it with counsel.
corrections_applied: Corrects old Move 04's treatment of the eighty per cent derate as a universal rule; it is a US continuous-load convention and the contract, not the convention, is what governs.

Separates the commercial power schedule from the physical cabinet arithmetic, which the previous manifest ran together in one Move and therefore signed before it had been calculated (that arithmetic is now Move 31).

reversible 'No' retained and now truthful, because this is where the first irreversible commitment in the Part is actually made — the objection the critic raised against old Move 02 carrying 'Immediately'.

title: What the service credit is actually worth
leaving: Cloud service-level agreements and their credits
hook: Establishes what the facility owes when it fails, which is a capped credit, and redirects the negotiation onto the derate, the power increase and the exit.
scope: Works out what the contract owes you when the facility fails, which is less than the reader expects. It reads the power and cooling service levels, the point of measurement, the exclusions for planned maintenance and force majeure, the window inside which a claim must be filed, and the cap: credits are almost always the sole and exclusive remedy and are almost always limited to a fraction of one month's recurring charge, so they will never approach the cost of an outage. The conclusion is that credits are a poor use of the negotiation, and that the same hours belong on the derate, the mid-term power increase and the exit. About three days.
corrections_applied: New Move: the previous manifest left the cloud SLA in the leaving list of nothing, so the reader moved from one capped credit regime to another without ever being told what either was worth.
leaving stated as the generic category rather than a named provider's SLA.

title: The notice period and the door out
hook: Fixes the term, the escalator, the auto-renewal notice and the relocation clause, and writes the exit as a runbook with its notice date in the calendar.
scope: Fixes the commercial shape of the agreement: the initial term and whether it matches the depreciation schedule the bill of materials assumed, the annual escalator, the auto-renewal and the notice required to stop it, and the conditions under which the facility may move you within the building or out of it. It writes the exit as a runbook rather than a clause — space returned to bare cabinet, cross-connects formally disconnected and their disconnection fees paid, the final invoice, and who does the de-racking. It ends with the notice date in the same calendar as everything else, because an agreement that rolls into a further term because nobody diarised a hundred and eighty days is the commonest way this saving disappears. About three days.
corrections_applied: New Move: old Move 02 promised 'a costed exit plan' for rented metal and nothing wrote the colocation exit, which is the more expensive of the two.
Closes the contract thread before any physical work starts, so the irreversible Moves in this Part are consecutive and identifiable rather than scattered.

title: The 80 per cent you are allowed to draw
hook: Turns the bill of materials into a per-cabinet power budget in the units the facility bills in, with outlets counted and the phases balanced.
scope: Turns the bill of materials into a per-cabinet power budget, in the units the facility bills in. It works the arithmetic explicitly: a 208 volt three-phase 30 amp feed is 10.8 kVA on the nameplate and about 8.6 kW once the US continuous-load derate is applied, while a 400 volt three-phase 32 amp European feed is 22.2 kVA and is sold against a different convention entirely. It counts PDU outlets rather than assuming them, because every server takes two, each switch takes two, and the C13 and C19 mix is fixed the day the strips are ordered. Ends with a phase-balanced cabinet plan that leaves headroom for the machines added in year two. About four days.
corrections_applied: Splits the physical arithmetic out of old Move 04, which signed a contract and sized the cabinet in the same Move and therefore did neither in the right order.
States both the US and the European feed arithmetic rather than presenting the eighty per cent derate as a single universal number.
Every physical Move after this one depends on it, which the previous manifest's dependency graph did not express.

title: Two feeds, one of which you have tested
hook: Establishes that a dual-fed cabinet is worth one feed at the derate, puts single-supply equipment behind a transfer switch, and pulls the A feed to prove it.
scope: Takes the A and B feeds seriously. The usable budget of a dual-fed cabinet is one feed at the derate rather than the sum of the two, so a pair of 8.6 kW feeds is an 8.6 kW cabinet and each PDU runs near forty per cent in normal operation. It deals with the equipment that has a single power supply — a console server, a cheap access switch, an out-of-band unit — by putting it behind a rack transfer switch instead of choosing a feed and hoping. Then it pulls the A feed with the cabinet fully loaded and nothing yet depending on it, and measures what the B feed actually carried and what tripped. About three days, one of which is the test.
corrections_applied: New Move: old Move 04 planned A and B feeds into dual supplies and never tested one, and never stated that the two feeds do not add.
Placed while nothing depends on the cabinet, which is the only moment at which pulling a feed is free.

title: The inlet temperature you are allowed
hook: Commits the inlet temperature at the top of the cabinet inside containment, then fixes the blanking, brush strips and aisle orientation that make it achievable.
scope: Gets the cooling commitment written down at the point that matters — inlet air at the top of the cabinet inside containment, not a room average taken at the cooling unit's return. It sets the envelope against the ASHRAE classes rather than folklore: 18 to 27 degrees is the recommended envelope, mainstream class A2 equipment is allowable to 35, and the facility's density limit per cabinet is usually the binding constraint rather than any temperature. It then fixes the airflow discipline that makes the number achievable: consistent hot and cold aisle orientation, blanking panels in every unused rack unit, brush strips on cable cut-outs, and no cabinet drawing its air from the hot aisle. About three days, including a thermal survey done with a probe rather than a hand.
corrections_applied: New Move: cooling appeared in the previous manifest only as a phrase in old Move 04's leaving list, with no committed inlet temperature and no measurement point.
Runs before racking, because airflow discipline is designed into the cabinet layout in Move 36 rather than added to it afterwards.

title: The importer of record and the loading dock
hook: Names the importer of record, settles the customs and import-VAT position, and books the dock, the lift and the window against a cabinet approaching a tonne.
scope: Gets the hardware into the building both legally and physically. The legal half: a colocation provider will not act as importer of record, because that puts its name on a customs debt for equipment it does not own, so you need an entity with a customs registration in the destination country — an EORI number in the UK or EU — and a broker who has read your commercial invoice before the pallet flies. Servers classify under heading 8471 and generally attract no duty under the Information Technology Agreement, but import VAT falls due on the landed value, only the named importer can recover it, and origin-based tariffs can override the headline rate. The physical half: booked delivery window, dock hours, lift capacity against a cabinet approaching a tonne, whether racks arrive on pallets that will not fit a passenger lift, and where the packaging goes afterwards. About five days of work spread across six weeks of lead time.
corrections_applied: New Move: the previous manifest moved from a purchase order in old Move 01 to a racked cabinet in old Move 04 with nothing in between, and import is where hardware programmes stall for weeks.
Runs in parallel with the facility work rather than after it, because its six weeks of lead time otherwise sit on the critical path to Move 36.

title: Who can get in at 03:00
leaving: The shared-responsibility split for physical security
hook: Settles the access list, the escort rules and a remote-hands agreement measured in ticket-to-touch, and ends with a ticket template a stranger can follow.
scope: Answers the question in both directions. Inward: the named access list and how fast a leaver comes off it, escort rules for contractors, whether the cabinet is locked and who holds the second key, camera coverage and retention, and the plain fact that facility staff can open your cabinet whatever the contract says — which is why Move 48 puts disk encryption and key custody underneath everything that follows. Outward: the remote hands agreement, measured in ticket-to-touch rather than response time, billed in fifteen-minute increments, with an escalation ladder that has a name and a telephone number at the top. Because the technician does exactly what the ticket says and no more, the Move ends with a ticket template carrying photographs, cabinet, rack unit and port number. About three days.
corrections_applied: Keeps old Move 04's remote-hands contract and gives it the inward half it never had, which is what makes the encryption requirement in Move 48 an argument rather than an assertion.

title: The first rack
hook: Racks the first cabinet in the order that survives contact with the second: strips first, weight low, gaps blanked, and photographs before any data cable.
scope: Racks the first cabinet in the order that survives contact with the second one: PDUs and cable management before anything heavy, switches placed where the cabling plan wants them rather than at the top out of habit, the heaviest chassis low, rails checked against the actual cabinet depth, and a rack-unit budget that has already counted the strips, the patch panels and the console server. It leaves deliberate gaps for year two instead of filling to the last unit, and blanks every one of them. Ends with the cabinet powered, the out-of-band network reachable from outside the building, and photographs of the front and rear taken before a single data cable is added. About one week for two people, most of it on site.

title: Labels, port maps and the as-built
hook: Builds the label scheme, port map and as-built that let somebody who has never entered the room replace the correct part at three in the morning.
scope: Builds the documentation that lets somebody who has never entered the room replace the correct part at three in the morning. A label scheme that survives a machine being moved because it names the position rather than the server, both ends of every cable labelled, a port map tying switch port to cabinet, rack unit and interface, and serial numbers recorded against positions, so that the drive that fails in Move 111 can be found by its bay. The test of the document is the second site: hand it to a supplier in another city and see whether they can build the same cabinet from it without ringing you. About four days, and the cheapest four days in this Part.

title: The drives that leave, and the snapshots that stay
leaving: Provider-managed snapshot, image and backup retention
hook: Sanitises the drives that leave against serial-level certificates and destroys the key material behind the snapshots, images and vaults that stay.
scope: Ends the old estate on both sides of the migration. On hardware you hold, sanitisation follows NIST SP 800-88, reissued as Revision 2 in September 2025 and now deferring technique to IEEE 2883-2022: cryptographic erase for self-encrypting media, the drive's own sanitise command for NVMe, and physical destruction only where the data classification or a contract demands it, because multi-pass overwriting an SSD is theatre when wear levelling and over-provisioning keep cells out of reach of the write path. Every unit leaves against a certificate listing serial numbers, under a chain of custody, through a processor whose certification you have checked, with a disposal note that satisfies your waste-electricals obligation. On the cloud side you will never hold the platter, so the lever is the key: destroy the key material, then delete the snapshots, images, object versions and backup vaults, and allow for soft-delete windows and purge protection that make deletion complete days after you asked for it. About one week.
corrections_applied: New Move: the previous manifest deleted nothing until old Move 72 closed the account, leaving snapshots, images and backup vaults live throughout, and never addressed the physical drives at all.

Updated to NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, published 26 September 2025, which withdraws Revision 1 and refers technique to IEEE 2883-2022 rather than carrying its own per-device tables; both facts verified against the NIST announcement.
Corrects the widespread multi-pass-overwrite instruction, which does not sanitise flash, and states the cloud-side mechanism as key destruction rather than deletion.
Supplies the sanitisation certificates that Move 119's auditor asks for, a dependency the previous manifest's audit Move could not have satisfied.

title: The management VLAN, and the way in at 03:00

title: Talos as the host OS, and where it cannot go
leaving: Managed node images and their patch and time-sync agents
hook: Commits to Talos as the host OS, names the two cases it cannot take, and sets the time-sync, conntrack, hugepage and interrupt defaults the managed image provided.
scope: Talos is the host OS: an API-only machine with no shell, no package manager and no SSH, configured entirely by a machine config that also carries time sync, conntrack and neighbour-table sizing, inotify limits, transparent hugepages, C-states and IRQ affinity, each with the symptom you get when it is wrong. There are two places Talos genuinely cannot go — an agent that requires a shell or a host package, and an out-of-tree DKMS driver — and in both cases the workload runs on the hypervisor tier of Move 70 or on a small labelled non-Talos pool, written into the runbook rather than discovered later. The images this replaces are Bottlerocket or Amazon Linux 2023 with SSM Patch Manager, Container-Optimized OS with automatic node upgrades, and AKS Ubuntu or Azure Linux with node image upgrades; a Container-Optimized OS reader has the shortest agent audit because that image was already immutable and shell-restricted, while an AKS reader most often carries a general-purpose distribution with a full agent estate. About 1 week.

The two genuine Talos exceptions are named in a line and given a landing (Move 70) instead of being used to reopen the OS choice
Leaving list genericised; the managed image and patch agent on all three clouds named in scope
Refiled from 'Ground' into Part III

title: Netboot, node identity and failure-domain labels
leaving: Golden machine images, launch templates and the instance metadata service
hook: Netboots nodes from a per-MAC record that also carries node identity and the rack, PDU and switch labels every later spread constraint reads.

The same per-MAC record carries node identity now that no metadata service issues it, and the rack, PDU and switch labels that make an inherited zone anti-affinity rule something other than a no-op, which is worth checking hardest on Azure, where availability zones are mapped per subscription and zone 1 in two subscriptions need not be the same physical zone. About 2 weeks.

title: Cilium, with kube-proxy off
leaving: The cloud-provider CNI plug-in and kube-proxy
hook: Installs Cilium with kube-proxy replaced, which ends the address accounting behind pod density and turns service resolution into a hash-map lookup.

The alternative for an old kernel is Calico's standard iptables dataplane, not its eBPF dataplane, which needs a newer kernel rather than an older one — 5.3 and above, with several features needing 5.8 — so the question only arises on the non-Talos exception from Move 41. Readers leaving the Amazon VPC CNI change datapath and address model at once, while GKE Dataplane V2 and Azure CNI Powered by Cilium are already Cilium, so those readers are mainly taking over a control loop somebody else ran. About 1 week.

About 1 week.

title: Local NVMe, and the default StorageClass nobody gave you
leaving: Managed network block storage and its default StorageClass
hook: Puts databases on local NVMe with power-loss protection, keeps replication in the application, and marks a default StorageClass so PVCs stop hanging Pending.
scope: Talos user volumes and the local static provisioner, filesystem and mount options, WaitForFirstConsumer binding, and the power-loss-protection requirement from Move 09 that everything in Part V rests on. Local volumes come first because Ceph sits on top of them in Move 49 while etcd and a single-writer database stay underneath, and the consequence is that a local volume pins its pod to that machine, which is what makes the drain arithmetic in Move 109 and the failed disk in Move 111 non-trivial. Reversibility is not immediate: the default StorageClass can be flipped back in a minute, but moving a bound volume off local NVMe is a data migration with a write-stop, so the point of no return is the first bound PVC. Recent EKS shipped no default StorageClass at all while GKE and AKS both did, so the Pending PVC is a familiar surprise to one of the three readers and a new one to the other two; the work is about 1 week.

title: Encryption at rest, and who holds the key
leaving: Default encryption at rest on managed volumes
hook: Encrypts the state and ephemeral partitions and the Ceph OSDs, and settles who holds the key when the only copy of it lives on the cluster it unlocks.
scope: LUKS2 on the Talos STATE and EPHEMERAL partitions with the key provider chosen deliberately — node ID for convenience, TPM 2.0 to bind a disk to the machine it was installed in, or an external KMS server, noting that a KMS-sealed STATE partition cannot take its network configuration from the machine config because it needs the network before it unlocks. Ceph OSDs are created encrypted in Move 49 because encrypting them afterwards is a rebuild, and the Kubernetes secrets EncryptionConfiguration gets a key with a named custodian, which matters because Move 35 has already established that facility staff can open the cabinet. On two of the three clouds this was a control — EBS default encryption with KMS, Azure Storage Service Encryption with disk encryption sets — while Google encrypted every disk with a Google-managed key whether or not anyone asked, so a Google reader has a default to replace rather than a setting to port. There is no in-place decryption, so the point of no return is the first node installed with encryption enabled; about 1 week.
